title: Majestic Win
reviewNotes: Two source branches from seven-piece diagrams after Qxb5 at 69s and Kxb5 at 109s. Bd3/Qxd3/Nc5 and Be8/Qxe8/Nd6 pin then fork the queen; exact later knight-and-pawn endings win. Earlier ten-piece setup and larger rook/pawn sacrifices are source context. Capturing the bishop is a selected source reply, not an assertion that every defense is forced. The compressed later king marches are not encoded.
transcript: In this position, every single white piece is hanging to one [music] of the black pieces. And although you can maybe save one of them after black moves, there is still going to be a double attack on the other [music] pieces, which means that you're going to lose one of them. And once black stops the promotion, this is going to be completely lost. So, is this it? Is black simply winning in this position? Well, not exactly. You see, this is actually a position that I have composed myself. After researching, studying, and deconstructing literally hundreds of chess compositions, I have assembled all that I have learned in one utterly majestic study. And what I want this chess composition to teach you all is that when you're supposed to lose something, you should at least try to lose it on your own terms. Rook takes c6 is a majestic and brilliant sacrifice. Of course, this is a fork of the king and the queen. So, the queen really has to take. And the whole [music] point of that move was to lure the queen into another fork with pawn to b5. The king and the queen are both attacked. So, black really doesn't have any other choice but to capture the pawn. But if the queen takes, it seems as though the knight is still hanging, and now we've even lost the rook. But white has a majestic follow-up thanks to the incredible bishop d3. With the knight hanging, white gives up the other minor piece at the same time. But this does create a pin of the queen on the king, which means that the queen really has to take the bishop. But this sacrifice was not for nothing. The queen and the king are now placed in the perfect position to deliver a knight fork, forcing the king to move, winning the queen, and then running towards promotion, winning the game. But wait a second, because black also had the option of capturing the pawn with the king. But fate really smiles upon this position because the bishop and the knight are perfectly coordinated to deliver the same idea with Bishop to E8. This again pins the queen to the king. The queen takes and knight to D6 is another fork, which will allow white to win the game. And although the king is closer, he's still too far away to stop the pawn. White will win this game. And I would like to call my first ever chess composition majestic win.
